paññāya.dpd: wisdom; knowledge; understanding; insight; distinctive knowledge
paññāya.note: Here paññāya is genitive: paṭilābho paññāya, “the acquisition of wisdom”.

en: One may live a hundred years
with no sīla and no samādhi.
Better it is a single day of life
for one who has sīla and meditates.
He rejoices here, he rejoices hereafter,
one who does good rejoices in both places.
He rejoices and is happy,
seeing the purity of his own deeds.
He is delighted here, he is delighted hereafter,
one who does good is delighted in both places.
[When thinking] “I have done good,” he is delighted,
when gone to a good destination, he is delighted even more.
All tremble at violence;
all fear death.
Seeing oneself in others,
one would neither kill nor cause another to kill.
All tremble at violence;
life is dear to all.
Seeing oneself in others,
one would neither kill nor cause another to kill.
Happiness is virtue until life’s end,
happiness is confidence well established,
happiness is the acquisition of wisdom,
and happiness is the avoidance of wrongdoing.

pali: dhīro pūrati puññassa, thokaṃ thokam’pi ācinaṃ.
en: Do not underestimate the good, thinking: “This will not come
to me.” Drop by drop, the water pot becomes full.
So too, the wise person fills himself with good,
gathering it little by little.
The non-doing of all bad actions,
the performance of the wholesome,
and the purification of one’s mind —
this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
the killing of beings.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
the taking of what is not given.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
sexual misconduct.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from
false speech.
I undertake the training precept of abstention from alcohol
and [other] intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One,
the fully Enlightened One.
I go for refuge to the Buddha.
I go for refuge to the Dhamma.
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
By practicing in accordance with the Dhamma:
I venerate the Buddha;
I venerate the Dhamma;
I venerate the Saṅgha.
The Buddhas of the past,
the Buddhas of the future,
the Buddhas of the present —
I always pay respects.
The Dhammas of the past,
the Dhammas of the future,
the Dhammas of the present —
I always pay respects.
The Saṅghas of the past,
the Saṅghas of the future,
the Saṅghas of the present —
I always pay respects.

bhagavato.dpd: Sublime One; Blessed One; Fortunate One; Auspicious One; epithet of the Buddha

en: That Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened,
accomplished in true knowledge and conduct,
fortunate, knower of the world,
unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed,
teacher of devas and humans,
the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.
The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One,
directly visible, immediate,
inviting one to come and see, applicable,
to be personally experienced by the wise.
The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples
is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way,
practicing the right way, practicing the proper way;
that is, the four pairs of persons,
the eight types of individuals — this Saṅgha
of the Blessed One’s disciples
is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality,
worthy of offerings, worthy of reverence,
the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
“When a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata,
on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by craving,
not obsessed by aversion, not obsessed by delusion;
on that occasion his mind is simply straight,
based on the Tathāgata.
A noble disciple whose mind is straight gains inspiration
in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma,
gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
When he is joyful, rapture arises.
For one with a rapturous mind,
the body becomes tranquil.
One tranquil in body feels pleasure.
For one feeling pleasure,
the mind becomes concentrated.
This is called a noble disciple who dwells in balance
amid an unbalanced population,
who dwells unafflicted amid an afflicted population.
As one who has entered the stream of the Dhamma,
he develops recollection of the Buddha.
Again, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the
Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the
Blessed One…’
… recollects the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the
Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way…’”
“In a forest, at the foot of a tree,
or in an empty hut, O bhikkhus,
you should recollect the Buddha —
no fear will then arise in you.
But if you cannot recall the Buddha,
best in the world, the bull of men,
then you should recall the Dhamma,
emancipating, well expounded.
But if you cannot recall the Dhamma,
emancipating, well expounded,
then you should recall the Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit.
For those who thus recall the Buddha,
the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, bhikkhus,
no fear or trepidation will arise,
nor will their hair stand on end.”

pali: katame pañca? assutaṃ suṇāti; sutaṃ pariyodāpeti;
ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca ānisaṃsā dhamma-ssavane”ti.
en: “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in listening to the
Dhamma. What five? One hears what one has not heard;
one clarifies what has been heard; one overcomes
perplexity; one straightens out one’s view;
one’s mind becomes bright, calm and confident.
These are the five benefits in listening to the Dhamma.”

pali: ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ,
nigrodh’ārāme. atha kho mahānāmo sakko yena bhagavā
en: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among
the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park. Then
Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One,

pali: nisīdi. ekam antaṃ nisinno kho, mahānāmo sakko
en: paid homage to him, sat down to one side,
and said to him:
“Venerable sir, in what way is one a lay follower?”

pali: “yato kho, mahānāma, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti,
dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti
en: “When, Mahānāma, one has gone for refuge to
the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,
one is then a lay follower.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in virtue?”

pali: “yato kho, mahānāma, upāsako pāṇ’ātipātā paṭivirato hoti,
ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako sīla-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: “When, Mahānāma, a lay follower abstains from the
destruction of life, from taking what is not given,
from sexual misconduct, from false speech,
and from wines, liquor, and intoxicants that are
a basis for negligence, the lay follower is
accomplished in virtue.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in devotion?”
“Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower is devoted;
he has confidence in the enlightenment of the
Tathāgata thus:
‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened,
accomplished in true knowledge and conduct,
fortunate, knower of the world,

pali: ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako saddhā-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed,
teacher of devas and humans,
the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’
In that way a lay follower is accomplished in devotion.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in generosity?”

pali: ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako cāga-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: “Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower dwells at home with
a mind devoid of the stain of stinginess,
freely generous, open-handed, delighting in
relinquishment, one devoted to charity,
delighting in giving and sharing. In that way a lay
follower is accomplished in generosity.”
“In what way, venerable sir, is a lay follower
accomplished in wisdom?”

pali: ettāvatā kho, mahānāma, upāsako paññā-sampanno hotī”ti.
en: “Here, Mahānāma, a lay follower is wise,
he possesses wisdom directed to arising and
passing away, which is noble and penetrative,
leading to the complete destruction of dukkha.
In that way a lay follower is accomplished in wisdom.”
“There are, bhikkhus, these five gifts, great gifts,
primal, of long standing, traditional, ancient,
unsullied and never before sullied,
which are not being sullied, and will not be sullied,
not rejected by wise ascetics and brahmins.

pali: katamāni pañca? idha, bhikkhave, ariya-sāvako pāṇ’ātipātaṃ
pahāya, pāṇ’ātipātā paṭivirato hoti. pāṇ’ātipātā paṭivirato,
abhayaṃ deti, averaṃ deti, abyābajjhaṃ deti.
en: What five? Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned
the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction
of life. By abstaining from the destruction of life,
the noble disciple gives to an immeasurable number
of beings freedom from fear, enmity, and affliction.

pali: aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā, averaṃ datvā,
idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ dānaṃ mahā-dānaṃ … pe …
en: Having given to an immeasurable number of beings
freedom from fear, enmity, and affliction,
he himself in turn enjoys immeasurable freedom
from fear, enmity, and affliction.
This is the first gift, a great gift …

pali: puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, ariya-sāvako adinn’ādānaṃ pahāya
en: Again, a noble disciple, having abandoned the taking
of what is not given, abstains from taking what is not
given … abstains from sexual misconduct … abstains
from false speech … abstains from liquor, wine, and
intoxicants, the basis for negligence.
By abstaining from liquor, wine, and intoxicants,
the basis for negligence, the noble disciple gives
to an immeasurable number of beings freedom
from fear, enmity, and affliction.

pali: aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā, averaṃ datvā,
abyābajjhassa bhāgī hoti. idaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcamaṃ dānaṃ,
asaṃkiṇṇaṃ, asaṃkiṇṇa-pubbaṃ, na saṃkiyati na saṃkiyissati,
en: He himself in turn enjoys immeasurable freedom
from fear, enmity, and affliction. This is the fifth gift,
a great gift, primal, of long standing, traditional,
ancient, unsullied and never before sullied,
which is not being sullied and will not be
sullied, not rejected by wise ascetics and
brahmins.”
“Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!
It is possible to abandon the unwholesome.

pali: no ce’daṃ, bhikkhave, sakkā abhavissa akusalaṃ pajahituṃ,
en: If it were not possible to abandon the unwholesome,
I would not say:
‘Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!’

pali: yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, sakkā akusalaṃ pajahituṃ,
en: But because it is possible to abandon the
unwholesome, I say:
‘Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!’

pali: akusalañ ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave, pahīnaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya
en: If this abandoning of the unwholesome led to harm
and dukkha, I would not tell you to abandon it.

pali: yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, akusalaṃ pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya
en: But because the abandoning of the unwholesome
leads to welfare and happiness,
I say: ‘Bhikkhus, abandon the unwholesome!’

pali: no ce’daṃ, bhikkhave, sakkā abhavissa kusalaṃ bhāvetuṃ,
yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, sakkā kusalaṃ bhāvetuṃ,
en: “Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!
It is possible to develop the wholesome.
If it were not possible to develop the wholesome,
I would not say: ‘Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!’
But because it is possible to develop the wholesome,
I say: ‘Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!’

pali: kusalañ ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvitaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya
‘kusalaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvethā’ti. yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave,
en: If this developing of the wholesome led to harm and
dukkha, I would not tell you to develop it.
But because the developing of the wholesome leads
to welfare and happiness,
I say: ‘Bhikkhus, develop the wholesome!’”

pali: “cattāro’me, bhikkhave, ariya-vaṃsā aggaññā, rattaññā, vaṃsaññā, porāṇā, asaṃkiṇṇā, asaṃkiṇṇa-pubbā, na saṃkīyanti na saṃkīyissanti, appaṭikuṭṭhā samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhi. katame cattāro?
en: “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages, primal, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unsullied and never before sullied, which are not being sullied and will not be sullied, which are not repudiated by wise ascetics and brahmins. What four?

pali: idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena cīvarena, itarītara-cīvara-santuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇa-vādī, na ca cīvara-hetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati; aladdhā ca cīvaraṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca cīvaraṃ agadhito, amucchito, anajjhosanno, ādīnava-dassāvī, nissaraṇa-pañño paribhuñjati;
en: (1) Here, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe, and he does not engage in a wrong search, in what is improper, for the sake of a robe. If he does not get a robe he is not agitated, and if he gets one he uses it without being tied to it, infatuated with it, and blindly absorbed in it, seeing the danger in it and understanding the escape from it.

pali: tāya ca pana itarītara-cīvara-santuṭṭhiyā n’ev’attān’ukkaṃseti, no paraṃ vambheti. yo hi tattha dakkho, analaso, sampajāno, patissato, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariya-vaṃse ṭhito.
en: Yet he does not extol himself or disparage others because of this. Any bhikkhu who is skillful in this, diligent, clearly comprehending and ever aware, is said to be standing in an ancient, primal noble lineage.

pali: puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena piṇḍa-pātena … pe … itarītarena sen’āsanena … pe … ariya-vaṃse ṭhito.
en: (2) Again, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of almsfood … (3) Again, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of lodging … is said to be standing in an ancient, primal noble lineage.

pali: puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhāvan’ārāmo hoti bhāvana-rato, pahān’ārāmo hoti pahāna-rato; tāya ca pana bhāvan’ārāmatāya bhāvana-ratiyā pahān’ārāmatāya pahāna-ratiyā n’ev’attān’ukkaṃseti, no paraṃ vambheti. yo hi tattha dakkho, analaso, sampajāno, patissato, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariya-vaṃse ṭhito.
en: (4) Again, a bhikkhu finds delight in development, is delighted with development, finds delight in abandoning, is delighted with abandoning. Yet he does not extol himself or disparage others because of this. Any bhikkhu who is skillful in this, diligent, clearly comprehending and ever aware, is said to be standing in an ancient, primal noble lineage.

pali: ime kho, bhikkhave, cattāro ariya-vaṃsā aggaññā, rattaññā, vaṃsaññā, porāṇā, asaṃkiṇṇā, asaṃkiṇṇa-pubbā, na saṃkīyanti na saṃkīyissanti, appaṭikuṭṭhā samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhi.
en: These, bhikkhus, are the four noble lineages, primal, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unsullied and never before sullied, which are not being sullied and will not be sullied, which are not repudiated by wise ascetics and brahmins.

pali: imehi ca pana, bhikkhave, catūhi ariya-vaṃsehi samannāgato bhikkhu puratthimāya ce’pi disāya viharati, sv’eva aratiṃ sahati, na taṃ arati sahati; pacchimāya ce’pi disāya viharati … uttarāya ce’pi disāya viharati … dakkhiṇāya ce’pi disāya viharati, sv’eva aratiṃ sahati, na taṃ arati sahati. taṃ kissa hetu? arati-rati-saho hi, bhikkhave, dhīro”ti.
en: Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu possesses these four noble lineages, if he dwells in the east he vanquishes discontent, discontent does not vanquish him; if he dwells in the west … in the north … in the south he vanquishes discontent, discontent does not vanquish him. For what reason? Because he is a steadfast one who vanquishes discontent and delight.”
Discontent does not vanquish the steadfast one,
[for] the steadfast one is not vanquished by discontent.
The steadfast one vanquishes discontent,
for the steadfast one is a vanquisher of discontent.
Who can obstruct the dispeller
who has discarded all kamma?
Who is fit to blame one who is like
a coin of refined gold?
Even the devas praise such a one;
by Brahmā too he is praised.

pali: evaṃ me sutaṃ. ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ
en: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was
dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

pali: atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā ten’upasaṅkami;
en: Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One,
paid homage to him, sat down to one side,

pali: ekam antaṃ nisinno kho, āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ
en: and said to him:
(1) “Venerable sir, what is the purpose and benefit of
wholesome virtuous behavior?”
(2) “Ānanda, the purpose and benefit of wholesome
virtuous behavior is non-regret.”
(3) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of
non-regret?”
“The purpose and benefit of non-regret is joy.”
(4) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of joy?”
“The purpose and benefit of joy is rapture.”
(5) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of
rapture?”
“The purpose and benefit of rapture is tranquility.”
(6) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of
tranquility?”
“The purpose and benefit of tranquility is pleasure.”
(7) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of
pleasure?”
“The purpose and benefit of pleasure is concentration.”
(8) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of
concentration?”
“The purpose and benefit of concentration is the
knowledge and vision of things as they really are.”
(9) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of the
knowledge and vision of things as they really are?”
“The purpose and benefit of the knowledge and vision of
things as they really are is disenchantment.”
(10) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of
disenchantment?”
“The purpose and benefit of disenchantment is
dispassion.”
(11) “And what, venerable sir, is the purpose and benefit of
dispassion?”
“The purpose and benefit of dispassion is the knowledge
and vision of liberation.

pali: iti kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlāni avippaṭisār’atthāni
en: Thus, Ānanda, (1)–(2) the purpose and benefit of
wholesome virtuous behavior is non-regret;
(3) the purpose and benefit of non-regret is joy;
(4) the purpose and benefit of joy is rapture;
(5) the purpose and benefit of rapture is tranquility;
(6) the purpose and benefit of tranquility is pleasure;
(7) the purpose and benefit of pleasure is concentration;
(8) the purpose and benefit of concentration is the
knowledge and vision of things as they really are;
(9) the purpose and benefit of the knowledge and vision
of things as they really are is disenchantment; (10) the
purpose and benefit of disenchantment is dispassion;

pali: iti kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlāni anupubbena aggāya
en: and (11) the purpose and benefit of dispassion is the
knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus, Ānanda, wholesome virtuous behavior progressively
leads to the foremost.”

pali: kathañ ca, bhikkhave, sammā-diṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti?
en: “Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first.
And how does right view come first?
One understands wrong action as wrong action and
right action as right action:
this is one’s right view. […]

pali: sā’ssa hoti sammā-sati. itiyime tayo dhammā
en: One makes an effort to abandon wrong action and to
enter upon right action: this is one’s right effort.
Aware, one abandons wrong action,
aware, one enters upon and abides in right action:
this is one’s right awareness.
Thus these three things run and circle around right
action, that is, right view, right effort, and right
awareness. …”
“Not associating with fools,
associating with the wise,
and venerating those worthy of veneration:
this is the highest blessing.
Residing in a suitable place,
merit done in the past,
and directing oneself rightly:
this is the highest blessing.
Much learning, a craft,
well-trained discipline,
and well-spoken speech:
this is the highest blessing.
Serving one’s mother and father,
supporting one’s wife and children,
and an honest occupation:
this is the highest blessing.
Giving and righteous conduct,
assistance to relatives,
blameless deeds:
this is the highest blessing.
Desisting and abstaining from bad actions,
refraining from intoxicating drink,
diligence in good qualities:
this is the highest blessing.
Reverence and humility,
contentment and gratitude,
timely listening to the Dhamma:
this is the highest blessing.
Patience, being amenable to advice,
the seeing of ascetics,
timely discussion on the Dhamma:
this is the highest blessing.
Ardent practice and the spiritual life,
seeing of the noble truths,
and realization of nibbāna:
this is the highest blessing.
One whose mind does not shake
when touched by worldly conditions,
sorrowless, stainless, secure:
this is the highest blessing.
Those who have done these things
are victorious everywhere;
everywhere they go safely:
theirs is that highest blessing.”
One should guard against angry speech,
let one be restrained in speech.
Abandoning verbal misconduct,
one should practice good conduct in speech.
One is not wise because one speaks much.
One who is peaceful,
kind and fearless
is called wise.
Just as a lovely flower, beautiful but without fragrance,
so too, well-spoken words bring no good results
for one who doesn’t act accordingly.
Just as a lovely flower, beautiful and fragrant,
so too, well-spoken words have good results
for one who acts accordingly.
Better than a thousand meaningless words
is a single meaningful word,
upon hearing which
one finds peace.

tatra.dpd: there; in that place; in that case

pali: “… evameva kho, rāja-kumāra, yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ
en: “… So too, prince, such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial,
and which is also unwelcome and disagreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yam’pi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
anattha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā,
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true and correct but unbeneficial,
and which is also unwelcome and disagreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yañ ca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
attha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā,
tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya.
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true, correct, and beneficial,
but which is unwelcome and disagreeable to others:
the Tathāgata knows the time to use such speech.

pali: yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ, atacchaṃ,
anattha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā,
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial,
but which is welcome and agreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yam’pi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
anattha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā,
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true and correct but unbeneficial,
and which is welcome and agreeable to others:
such speech the Tathāgata does not utter.

pali: yañ ca tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ,
attha-saṃhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā,
tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya.
en: Such speech as the Tathāgata knows
to be true, correct, and beneficial,
and which is welcome and agreeable to others:
the Tathāgata knows the time to use such speech.
Why is that?
Because the Tathāgata has compassion for beings.” […]

pali: “… na kho pan’etaṃ, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ patirūpaṃ
en: “… Bhikkhus, it is not suitable for you, respectable
people who have gone forth from the household life
into homelessness out of faith, to engage in various
kinds of pointless talk, that is: talk about kings,
thieves… wars; talk about food, drink, clothes… talk
about garlands and scents; talk about relatives,
vehicles, villages, towns… miscellaneous talk; tales
of land and sea; talk about becoming this or that.
There are, bhikkhus, these ten topics for discussion.
What ten? Talk on fewness of desires, contentment,
solitude, non-entanglement, arousing energy,
virtuous behavior, concentration, wisdom,
liberation, knowledge and vision of liberation.
These are the ten topics for discussion.”

no.note: Here no is the pronoun “our”, not the word for “not”.

en: “Bhikkhus, there are these five courses of speech
that others may use when they address you:
their speech may be timely or untimely,
true or untrue,
gentle or harsh,
connected with good or with harm,
spoken with a mind of mettā or with inner hate. […]

pali: hit’ānukampī ca viharissāma metta-cittā, na dos’antarā.
en: Herein, bhikkhus, you should train thus:
‘Our minds will remain unaffected, and we shall utter
no harmful words; compassionate for their welfare,
we shall dwell with a mind of mettā, without inner hate.

pali: tañ ca puggalaṃ mettā-sahagatena cetasā pharitvā
en: We shall dwell pervading that person with a mind
suffused with mettā, and starting with him,
we shall dwell pervading the all-encompassing world
with a mind suffused with mettā, abundant, exalted,
boundless, without hostility and without ill-will.’
That is how you should train, bhikkhus.

pali: tatr’āpi yo mano padūseyya, na me so tena sāsana-karo.
en: Bhikkhus, even if mean bandits were to sever you limb
by limb with a two-handled saw, one who gave rise to
a mind of hate towards them would not be acting
according to my teaching.

pali: ‘na c’eva no cittaṃ vipariṇataṃ bhavissati … pe …’
en: Herein, bhikkhus, you should train thus:
‘Our minds will remain unaffected …’
That is how you should train, bhikkhus.”

suttas.title: hadayaṅgamā vācā
suttas.en: Words That Go to the Heart

en: “… Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false
speech; he speaks truth, adheres to truth;
he is trustworthy and reliable, no deceiver of the world.
This, too, is there in his sīla.

pali: pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāya, pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti;
ito sutvā, na amutra akkhātā, imesaṃ bhedāya;
amutra vā sutvā, na imesaṃ akkhātā, amūsaṃ bhedāya.
en: Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from
divisive speech; if he hears something here, he does not
repeat it elsewhere in order to divide [those people] from
these; if he hears something elsewhere, he does not repeat
it to these people here, in order to divide them from those;

pali: iti bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātā, sahitānaṃ vā anuppadātā,
en: thus he is one who reunites those who are divided,
a promoter of unity, who enjoys harmony,
rejoices in harmony, delights in harmony,
a speaker of words that promote harmony.
This, too, is there in his sīla.

pali: pharusaṃ vācaṃ pahāya, pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato
hoti; yā sā vācā nelā, kaṇṇa-sukhā,
en: Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh
speech; he speaks words that are gentle,
pleasing to the ear, lovable, words that go to the heart,
courteous words that are cherished by many people
and agreeable to many people.
This, too, is there in his sīla.

pali: vinaya-vādī, nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā hoti, kālena,
en: Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle
chatter; he speaks at a proper time, speaks what is truthful,
speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma,
speaks on the discipline; at the proper time he speaks
such words as are worth treasuring, reasonable,
to the point, and beneficial.
This, too, is there in his sīla.”
Regard the one who sees your faults
as a guide to hidden treasure;
associate with such a wise one
who points out your mistakes.
It is better, not worse,
to associate with such a wise person.

assa.dpd: could be; may be; might be; should be
assa.note: evam assa: “it may be thus”, i.e. if this occurs to you. Elsewhere assa is the pronoun “his”.

en: “While you are training in harmony,
with mutual appreciation, without disputing,
some bhikkhu might commit an offence or a transgression.
Now, bhikkhus, you should not hurry to criticize him;
rather, the person should be examined thus: (1)
‘I shall not be troubled
and the other person will not be hurt;
for the other person is not angry and resentful,
he is not firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes easily,

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: and I can make that person emerge from the
unwholesome and establish him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (2)
‘I shall not be troubled,
but the other person will be hurt;
for the other person is angry and resentful.
However, he is not firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes easily,
and I can make that person emerge from the
unwholesome and establish him in the wholesome.

pali: atha kho etadeva bahutaraṃ — so’haṃ sakkomi etaṃ
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: It is a minor matter that the other person will be hurt,
but it is a much greater thing that I can make that
person emerge from the unwholesome and establish
him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (3)
‘I shall be troubled,
but the other person will not be hurt;
for the other person is not angry and resentful,
though he is firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes with difficulty;
yet I can make that person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.

pali: mayhaṃ vihesā. atha kho etadeva bahutaraṃ —
so’haṃ sakkomi etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: It is a minor matter that I shall be troubled,
but it is a much greater thing that I can make that
person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: sakkomi c’āhaṃ etaṃ puggalaṃ akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvā
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (4)
‘I shall be troubled and the other person will be hurt;
for the other person is angry and resentful,
and he is firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes with difficulty;
yet I can make that person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.

pali: atha kho etadeva bahutaraṃ — so’haṃ sakkomi etaṃ
sace, bhikkhave, evam assa, kallaṃ vacanāya.
en: It is a minor matter that I shall be troubled and the other
person hurt, but it is a much greater thing that I can
make that person emerge from the unwholesome
and establish him in the wholesome.’
If such occurs to you, bhikkhus, it is proper to speak.

pali: daḷha-diṭṭhī duppaṭinissaggī, na c’āhaṃ sakkomi etaṃ
en: Then it may occur to you, bhikkhus: (5)
‘I shall be troubled and the other person will be hurt;
for the other person is angry and resentful,
and he is firmly attached to his view
and he relinquishes with difficulty;
and I cannot make that person emerge from the
unwholesome and establish him in the wholesome.’
One should not underrate equanimity towards
such a person.”

pali: “pañca kho ime, bhāradvāja, dhammā diṭṭh’eva dhamme
pañca dhammā diṭṭh’eva dhamme dvedhā vipākā.
en: “There are five things, Bhāradvāja, that may turn out in
two different ways here and now. What five?
Faith, liking, oral tradition, logical reasoning,
and reflective acceptance of a view. These five things may
turn out in two different ways here and now.

pali: tañ ca hoti rittaṃ, tucchaṃ, musā;
tañ ca hoti bhūtaṃ, tacchaṃ, anaññathā.
en: Now something may be fully accepted out of faith,
yet it may be empty, hollow, and false;
but something else may not be fully accepted out of faith,
yet it may be factual, true, and unmistaken.

pali: api ca, bhāradvāja, surucitaṃyeva hoti … pe …
… pe … sunijjhāyitaṃyeva hoti, tañ ca hoti rittaṃ,
tucchaṃ, musā; no ce’pi sunijjhāyitaṃ hoti,
tañ ca hoti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anaññathā.
en: Again, something may be liked very much …
well transmitted … well cogitated …
well reflected upon, yet it may be empty, hollow,
and false; but something else may not be well reflected
upon, yet it may be factual, true, and unmistaken.
[Under these conditions] it is not proper for a wise man
who protects truth to come to the definite conclusion:
‘Only this is true, anything else is wrong.’”
“But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the protection
of truth? How does one protect truth?
We ask Master Gotama about the protection of truth.”

pali: ‘evaṃ me saddhā’ti — iti vadaṃ saccam anurakkhati,
na tveva tāva ek’aṃsena niṭṭhaṃ gacchati:
en: “If a person has faith, Bhāradvāja, he protects truth when
he says: ‘My faith is thus’;
but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:
‘Only this is true, anything else is wrong.’
In this way, Bhāradvāja, there is the protection of truth;
in this way he protects truth;
in this way we describe the protection of truth;
but as yet there is no awakening to truth.

pali: ruci ce’pi, bhāradvāja, purisassa hoti … pe …
anussavo ce’pi, bhāradvāja, purisassa hoti … pe …
ākāra-parivitakko ce’pi, bhāradvāja, purisassa hoti … pe …
na tveva tāva ek’aṃsena niṭṭhaṃ gacchati:
en: If a person has a liking for something … if he receives an
oral tradition … if he uses logical reasoning …
if he gains a reflective acceptance of a view,
he protects truth when he says:
‘My reflective acceptance of a view is thus’;
but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:
‘Only this is true, anything else is wrong.’
In this way too, Bhāradvāja, there is the protection of
truth; in this way he protects truth;
in this way we describe the protection of truth. …”

pali: kathañ ca, bhikkhave, sammā-diṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti?
en: “Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first.
And how does right view come first?
One understands wrong speech as wrong speech and
right speech as right speech:
this is one’s right view. […]

pali: upasampadāya; sv’āssa hoti sammā-vāyāmo. so sato
viharati; sā’ssa hoti sammā-sati. itiyime tayo dhammā
en: One makes an effort to abandon wrong speech and
to enter upon right speech: this is one’s right effort.
Aware, one abandons wrong speech,
aware, one enters upon and abides in right speech:
this is one’s right awareness. Thus these three things
run and circle around right speech, that is, right view,
right effort, and right awareness. …”

SECTIONS.title: yoniso manasikāra
SECTIONS.sub: Reflecting upon and Examining the Dhamma

dhammā.note: Here dhammā are the states of mind behind what one does and says.

en: Mind precedes all actions,
mind is their leader, they are made by mind.
If a person speaks or acts with an impure mind,
dukkha follows them,
like the wheel of a cart follows the foot of the ox.
Mind precedes all actions,
mind is their leader, they are made by mind.
If a person speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows them,
like a shadow that never leaves.
Good is the taming of the mind,
swift and so hard to control;
going wherever it likes.
A tamed mind brings happiness.
Let the wise one guard the mind,
so difficult to see and very subtle;
going wherever it likes.
A guarded mind brings happiness.
Whatever [harm] an enemy may do to an enemy,
or a hater to a hater,
a mind directed wrongly
can do worse to oneself than that.
Whatever [good] a mother, a father,
or any other relative may do for one,
a mind directed rightly
can do one more good than that.
The bhikkhu who enjoys the Dhamma,
delights in the Dhamma, reflects on the Dhamma,
and recollects the Dhamma —
he does not fall away from the true Dhamma.

pali: “n’āhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ eka-dhammam’pi samanupassāmi yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ bahulī-kataṃ sukh’ādhivahaṃ hoti, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ. cittaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvitaṃ bahulī-kataṃ sukh’ādhivahaṃ hotī”ti.
en: “Bhikkhus, I do not see even one other thing that, when developed and cultivated, brings such happiness as the mind. The mind, when developed and cultivated, brings happiness.”

pali: “n’āhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ eka-dhammam’pi samanupassāmi yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ bahulī-kataṃ mahato atthāya saṃvattati, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ. cittaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvitaṃ bahulī-kataṃ mahato atthāya saṃvattatī”ti.
en: “Bhikkhus, I do not see even one other thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to such great good as the mind. The mind, when developed and cultivated, leads to great good.”

pali: “n’āhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ eka-dhammam’pi samanupassāmi yaṃ evaṃ dantaṃ mahato atthāya saṃvattati, yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ. cittaṃ, bhikkhave, dantaṃ mahato atthāya saṃvattatī”ti.
en: “Bhikkhus, I do not see even one other thing that when tamed leads to such great good as the mind. A tamed mind leads to great good.”

pali: “seyyathā’pi, bhikkhave, yāni kānici rukkha-jātānaṃ, phandano tesaṃ aggam akkhāyati, yadidaṃ mudutāya c’eva kammaññatāya ca; evam evaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, n’āññaṃ eka-dhammam’pi samanupassāmi yaṃ evaṃ bhāvitaṃ bahulī-kataṃ mudu ca hoti kammaññañ ca, yathayidaṃ cittaṃ. cittaṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvitaṃ bahulī-kataṃ mudu ca hoti kammaññañ ca hotī”ti.
en: “Bhikkhus, just as the phandana tree is declared to be the best of trees with respect to malleability and wieldiness, so too I do not see even one other thing that, when developed and cultivated, is so malleable and wieldy as the mind. A developed and cultivated mind is malleable and wieldy.”

pali: sātthā, sabyañjanā, kevala-paripuṇṇaṃ, parisuddhaṃ, brahma-cariyaṃ abhivadanti.
en: “And what, bhikkhus, is the wealth of learning?
Here, a noble disciple has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned.
Those teachings that are good in the beginning,
good in the middle, and good in the end,
with the right meaning and phrasing,
which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life — such teachings as these he has learned much of,
retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated,
and penetrated well with wisdom.
This is called the wealth of learning.”
(Mahākoṭṭhika:) “Friend, how many conditions are there for the arising of right view?”

pali: “dve kho, āvuso, paccayā sammā-diṭṭhiyā uppādāya: parato ca ghoso, yoniso ca manasi-kāro.
ime kho, āvuso, dve paccayā sammā-diṭṭhiyā uppādāyā”ti.
en: (Sāriputta:) “Friend, there are two conditions for the arising of right view:
the voice of another and wise attention.
These are the two conditions for the arising of right view.”

pali: evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno ariyassa aṭṭh’aṅgikassa maggassa uppādāya etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ, etaṃ
en: “Bhikkhus, this is the forerunner and precursor of the rising of the sun, that is, the dawn. So too, bhikkhus,
for a bhikkhu this is the forerunner and precursor for the arising of the Noble Eightfold Path,
that is, accomplishment in wise attention.

pali: yoniso-manasi-kāra-sampannass’etaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṃ: ariyaṃ aṭṭh’aṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvessati, ariyaṃ aṭṭh’aṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulī-karissati.”
en: When a bhikkhu is accomplished in wise attention,
it is to be expected that he will develop and cultivate this Noble Eightfold Path.”

pali: “jānato ahaṃ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato. kiñ ca, bhikkhave,
jānato kiñ ca passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi?
yoniso ca manasi-kāraṃ ayoniso ca manasi-kāraṃ.”
en: “Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the āsavas is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and see. Who knows and sees what?
Wise attention and unwise attention.”

bhagavato.dpd: Sublime One; Blessed One; Fortunate One; Auspicious One; epithet of the Buddha

tatra.dpd: in that case; in that regard; in this matter; in this connection

pali: loko ca aṭṭha loka-dhamme anuparivattati. katame aṭṭha?
ime kho, bhikkhave, aṭṭha loka-dhammā lokaṃ anuparivattanti, loko ca ime aṭṭha loka-dhamme anuparivattati.
en: “Bhikkhus, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions. What eight?
Gain and loss, fame and disrepute,
blame and praise, and pleasure and pain.
These eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.

pali: tatra, bhikkhave, ko viseso, ko adhippayāso,
en: Bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person meets
gain and loss, fame and disrepute,
blame and praise, and pleasure and pain.
An instructed noble disciple also meets
gain and loss, fame and disrepute,
blame and praise, and pleasure and pain.
What is the distinction, the disparity,
the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed ordinary person with regard
to this?”

pali: “bhagavaṃ-mūlakā no, bhante, dhammā, bhagavaṃ-nettikā, bhagavaṃ-paṭisaraṇā. sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho.
en: “Venerable sir, our Dhamma is rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and has the Blessed One as its refuge. It would be good if the Blessed One would clear up the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from him, the bhikkhus will remember it.”

pali: “tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. bhagavā etad avoca:
en: “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely.
I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:

pali: ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ lābho; so ca kho anicco dukkho vipariṇāma-dhammo’ti yathā-bhūtaṃ na-ppajānāti.
uppajjati alābho … pe … uppajjati yaso … uppajjati ayaso … uppajjati nindā … uppajjati pasaṃsā … uppajjati sukhaṃ … uppajjati dukkhaṃ, so na iti paṭisañcikkhati:
tañ ca kho aniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ, vipariṇāma-dhamman’ti
en: “(1) Bhikkhus, when an uninstructed ordinary person meets with gain, he does not reflect thus:

‘This gain that I have met is impermanent, dukkha, and subject to change.’ He does not understand it as it really is. (2) When he meets with loss … (3) … fame … (4) … disrepute … (5) … blame … (6) … praise …
(7) … pleasure … (8) … pain, he does not reflect thus:
‘This pain that I have met is impermanent,
dukkha, and subject to change.’
He does not understand it as it really is.
Gain obsesses his mind,
and loss obsesses his mind.
Fame obsesses his mind,
and disrepute obsesses his mind.
Blame obsesses his mind,
and praise obsesses his mind.
Pleasure obsesses his mind,
and pain obsesses his mind.

pali: so uppannaṃ lābhaṃ anurujjhati, alābhe paṭivirujjhati. uppannaṃ yasaṃ anurujjhati, ayase paṭivirujjhati.
uppannaṃ pasaṃsaṃ anurujjhati, nindāya paṭivirujjhati. uppannaṃ sukhaṃ anurujjhati, dukkhe paṭivirujjhati.
en: He is attracted to gain and repelled by loss.
He is attracted to fame and repelled by disrepute.
He is attracted to praise and repelled by blame.
He is attracted to pleasure and repelled by pain.
Thus involved with attraction and repulsion,
he is not freed from birth, from old age and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and misery; he is not freed from dukkha, I say.

pali: sutavato ca kho, bhikkhave, ariya-sāvakassa uppajjati lābho,
so iti paṭisañcikkhati: ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ lābho;
so ca kho anicco, dukkho, vipariṇāma-dhammo’ti
uppajjati alābho … pe … uppajjati yaso … uppajjati ayaso … uppajjati nindā … uppajjati pasaṃsā … uppajjati sukhaṃ … uppajjati dukkhaṃ, so iti paṭisañcikkhati:
tañ ca kho aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāma-dhamman’ti
en: But, bhikkhus, (1) when an instructed noble disciple meets with gain, he reflects thus: ‘This gain that I have met is impermanent, dukkha, and subject to change.’ He thus understands it as it really is.
(2) When he meets with loss … (3) … fame …
(4) … disrepute … (5) … blame … (6) … praise …
(7) … pleasure … (8) … pain, he reflects thus:
‘This pain that I have met is impermanent,
dukkha, and subject to change.’
He thus understands it as it really is.

pali: tassa lābho’pi cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhati,
en: Gain does not obsess his mind,
and loss does not obsess his mind.
Fame does not obsess his mind,
and disrepute does not obsess his mind.
Blame does not obsess his mind,
and praise does not obsess his mind.
Pleasure does not obsess his mind,
and pain does not obsess his mind.

pali: uppannaṃ yasaṃ n’ānurujjhati, ayase na-ppaṭivirujjhati. uppannaṃ pasaṃsaṃ n’ānurujjhati,
en: He is not attracted to gain or repelled by loss.
He is not attracted to fame or repelled by disrepute. He is not attracted to praise or repelled by blame.
He is not attracted to pleasure or repelled by pain.
Having thus discarded attraction and repulsion,
he is freed from birth, from old age and death,
from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and misery;
he is freed from dukkha, I say.

pali: ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, viseso, ayaṃ adhippayāso,
en: This, bhikkhus, is the distinction, the disparity,
the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed ordinary person.”

sato.note: sato is the genitive of santa, “being”, from atthi: bodhi-sattass’eva sato, “while I was still a bodhisatta”.

gacchati.dpd: goes; walks; moves; wanders around; travels

pali: evaṃ me sutaṃ. ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jeta-vane, anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
en: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There he addressed the bhikkhus thus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir!” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:

pali: “pubb’eva me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhi-sattass’eva sato etad ahosi:
‘yaṃ nūn’āhaṃ dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvā vitakke vihareyyan’ti.
en: “Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still only an unenlightened Bodhisatta,
it occurred to me: ‘Suppose that I divide my thoughts into two classes.

pali: so kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, yo c’āyaṃ kāma-vitakko,
yo ca byāpāda-vitakko, yo ca vihiṃsā-vitakko —
yo c’āyaṃ nekkhamma-vitakko, yo ca abyāpāda-vitakko,
en: Then I set on one side thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty,
and I set on the other side thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill-will,
and thoughts of non-cruelty.

pali: tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa, ātāpino, pahit’attassa viharato, uppajjati kāma-vitakko.
en: As I abided thus, diligent, ardent, and resolute,
a thought of sensual desire arose in me.

pali: so evaṃ pajānāmi: ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ kāma-vitakko.
para-byābādhāya’pi saṃvattati, ubhaya-byābādhāya’pi saṃvattati; paññā-nirodhiko, vighāta-pakkhiko,
en: I understood thus: ‘This thought of sensual desire has arisen in me. This leads to my own affliction,
to others’ affliction, and to the affliction of both;
it obstructs wisdom, causes difficulties,
and leads away from nibbāna.’

pali: ‘ubhaya-byābādhāya saṃvattatī’ti’pi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati;
‘paññā-nirodhiko, vighāta-pakkhiko, anibbāna-saṃvattaniko’ti’pi me, bhikkhave, paṭisañcikkhato abbhatthaṃ gacchati.
en: When I considered: ‘This leads to my own affliction,’ it subsided in me; when I considered: ‘This leads to others’ affliction,’
it subsided in me;
when I considered: ‘This leads to the affliction of both,’ it subsided in me; when I considered:
‘This obstructs wisdom, causes difficulties,
and leads away from nibbāna,’ it subsided in me.

pali: so kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, uppann’uppannaṃ kāma-vitakkaṃ pajahameva, vinodameva, byantameva naṃ akāsiṃ.
en: Whenever a thought of sensual desire arose in me,
I abandoned it, removed it, did away with it.

pali: tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, evaṃ appamattassa, ātāpino, pahit’attassa viharato, uppajjati byāpāda-vitakko … pe …
en: As I abided thus, diligent, ardent, and resolute,
a thought of ill-will arose in me …
a thought of cruelty arose in me.

pali: so evaṃ pajānāmi: ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ vihiṃsā-vitakko.
en: I understood thus: ‘This thought of cruelty has arisen in me. This leads to my own affliction,
to others’ affliction, and to the affliction of both;
it obstructs wisdom, causes difficulties,
and leads away from nibbāna.’

pali: so kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, uppann’uppannaṃ vihiṃsā-vitakkaṃ pajahameva, vinodameva, byantameva naṃ akāsiṃ.
en: When I considered thus… it subsided in me.
Whenever a thought of cruelty arose in me,
I abandoned it, removed it, did away with it.

pali: yaññadeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulam anuvitakketi anuvicāreti, tathā tathā nati hoti cetaso.
kāma-vitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulam anuvitakketi anuvicāreti, pahāsi nekkhamma-vitakkaṃ,
en: Bhikkhus, whatever a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon, that will become the inclination of his mind. If he frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of sensual desire, he has abandoned the thought of renunciation to cultivate the thought of sensual desire, and then his mind inclines to thoughts of sensual desire.

pali: byāpāda-vitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave … pe … vihiṃsā-vitakkaṃ ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bahulam anuvitakketi anuvicāreti,
en: … upon thoughts of ill-will… upon thoughts of cruelty, he has abandoned the thought of
non-cruelty to cultivate the thought of cruelty,
and then his mind inclines to thoughts of cruelty.”

pali: “pañc’imāni, bhikkhave, ṭhānāni abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbāni itthiyā vā purisena vā,
en: “Bhikkhus, there are these five themes that should frequently be reflected upon by a woman or a man,
by a householder or one gone forth.
What five?

pali: abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ itthiyā vā purisena vā, gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā.
en: (1) A woman or a man, a householder or one gone forth, should frequently reflect thus:
‘I am subject to old age; I am not exempt from old age.’

pali: abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ itthiyā vā purisena vā, gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā.
en: (2) A woman or a man, a householder or one gone forth, should frequently reflect thus:
‘I am subject to illness; I am not exempt from illness.’

pali: abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ itthiyā vā purisena vā, gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā.
en: (3) A woman or a man, a householder or one gone forth, should frequently reflect thus:
‘I am subject to death; I am not exempt from death.’

pali: ‘sabbehi me piyehi manāpehi nānā-bhāvo vinā-bhāvo’ti abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ itthiyā vā purisena vā, gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā.
en: (4) A woman or a man, a householder or one gone forth, should frequently reflect thus:
‘I must be parted and separated from everyone and everything dear and agreeable to me.’

pali: yaṃ kammaṃ karissāmi — kalyāṇaṃ vā pāpakaṃ vā — tassa dāyādo bhavissāmī’ti
abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ itthiyā vā purisena vā, gahaṭṭhena vā pabbajitena vā.”
en: (5) A woman or a man, a householder or one gone forth, should frequently reflect thus:
‘I am the owner of my kamma, the heir of my kamma;
I have kamma as my origin, kamma as my relative, kamma as my refuge; whatever kamma I will do,
good or bad, of that I will be the heir.’”

pali: ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā nātike viharati giñjak’āvasathe. tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi: “maraṇa-ssati, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulī-katā maha-pphalā hoti mah’ānisaṃsā, amat’ogadhā, amata-pariyosānā. kathaṃ bhāvitā ca, bhikkhave, maraṇa-ssati, kathaṃ bahulī-katā maha-pphalā hoti mah’ānisaṃsā, amat’ogadhā, amata-pariyosānā?
en: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the brick hall. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, awareness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and benefit, culminating in the deathless, having the deathless as its consummation. And how is this so?

pali: idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu divase nikkhante rattiyā patihitāya iti paṭisañcikkhati: ‘bahukā kho me paccayā maraṇassa: ahi vā maṃ ḍaṃseyya, vicchiko vā maṃ ḍaṃseyya, sata-padī vā maṃ ḍaṃseyya; tena me assa kāla-kiriyā, so mam’assa antarāyo. upakkhalitvā vā papateyyaṃ, bhattaṃ vā me bhuttaṃ byāpajjeyya, pittaṃ vā me kuppeyya, semhaṃ vā me kuppeyya, satthakā vā me vātā kuppeyyuṃ; tena me assa kāla-kiriyā, so mam’assa antarāyo’ti.
en: Here, bhikkhus, when day has receded and night has approached, a bhikkhu reflects thus: ‘I could die on account of many causes. A snake might bite me, or a scorpion or centipede might sting me, and I might die; that would be an obstacle for me. I might stumble and fall down, or my food might disagree with me, or my bile might become agitated, or my phlegm might become agitated, or sharp winds in me might become agitated, and I might die; that would be an obstacle for me.’

pali: tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ: ‘atthi nu kho me pāpakā akusalā dhammā appahīnā, ye me assu rattiṃ kālaṃ karontassa antarāyāyā’ti.
en: This bhikkhu should reflect thus: ‘Do I have any bad unwholesome qualities that have not been abandoned, which might become an obstacle for me if I were to die tonight?’

pali: sace, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paccavekkhamāno evaṃ jānāti: ‘atthi me pāpakā akusalā dhammā appahīnā, ye me assu rattiṃ kālaṃ karontassa antarāyāyā’ti, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tesaṃ yeva pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya adhimatto chando ca, vāyāmo ca, ussāho ca, ussoḷhī ca, appaṭivānī ca, sati ca, sampajaññañ ca karaṇīyaṃ.
en: If, upon review, the bhikkhu knows: ‘I have bad unwholesome qualities that have not been abandoned, which might become an obstacle for me if I were to die tonight,’ then he should put forth extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, enthusiasm, indefatigability, awareness, and clear comprehension to abandon those bad unwholesome qualities.

pali: seyyathā’pi, bhikkhave, āditta-celo vā āditta-sīso vā tass’eva celassa vā sīsassa vā nibbāpanāya adhimattaṃ chandañ ca, vāyāmañ ca, ussāhañ ca, ussoḷhiñ ca, appaṭivāniñ ca, satiñ ca, sampajaññañ ca kareyya; evam evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tena bhikkhunā tesaṃ yeva pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya adhimatto chando ca … sampajaññañ ca karaṇīyaṃ.
en: Just as one whose clothes or head had caught fire would put forth extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, enthusiasm, indefatigability, awareness, and clear comprehension to extinguish [the fire on] his clothes or head, so that bhikkhu should put forth extraordinary desire … and clear comprehension to abandon those bad unwholesome qualities.

pali: sace pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paccavekkhamāno evaṃ jānāti: ‘n’atthi me pāpakā akusalā dhammā appahīnā, ye me assu rattiṃ kālaṃ karontassa antarāyāyā’ti, tena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā ten’eva pīti-pāmojjena vihātabbaṃ, aho-ratt’ānusikkhinā kusalesu dhammesu.
en: But if, upon review, the bhikkhu knows thus: ‘I do not have any bad unwholesome qualities that have not been abandoned, which might become an obstacle for me if I were to die tonight,’ then he should dwell in that same rapture and joy, training day and night in wholesome qualities.

pali: idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu rattiyā nikkhantāya divase patihite iti paṭisañcikkhati: ‘bahukā kho me paccayā maraṇassa … pe … ye me assu divā kālaṃ karontassa antarāyāyā’ti … pe …
en: But when night has receded and day has approached, a bhikkhu reflects thus: ‘I could die on account of many causes … which might become an obstacle for me if I were to die this day?’ …

pali: evaṃ bhāvitā kho, bhikkhave, maraṇa-ssati, evaṃ bahulī-katā maha-pphalā hoti mah’ānisaṃsā, amat’ogadhā, amata-pariyosānā”ti.
en: It is, bhikkhus, when awareness of death is developed and cultivated in this way that it is of great fruit and benefit, culminating in the deathless, having the deathless as its consummation.”

pali: kathañ ca, bhikkhave, sammā-diṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti? micchā-saṅkappaṃ, ‘micchā-saṅkappo’ti pajānāti,
en: “Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first.
And how does right view come first?
One understands wrong intention as wrong intention and right intention as right intention:
this is one’s right view. […]

pali: sā’ssa hoti sammā-sati. itiyime tayo dhammā
sammā-saṅkappaṃ anuparidhāvanti anuparivattanti, seyyath’idaṃ: sammā-diṭṭhi, sammā-vāyāmo, sammā-sati. …”
en: One makes an effort to abandon wrong intention and to enter upon right intention: this is one’s right effort. Aware, one abandons wrong intention,
aware, one enters upon and abides in right intention:
this is one’s right awareness. Thus these three things run and circle around right intention, that is, right view, right effort, and right awareness. …”
People go to many places for refuge —
to mountains and forests,
parks and tree shrines,
when they are startled by fear.
This is not a safe refuge,
this is not the highest refuge.
Not by going to this refuge
is one liberated from all dukkha.

pali: yo ca buddhañ ca dhammañ ca,
en: But one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha,
the Dhamma and the Saṅgha,
who sees the Four Noble Truths
with perfect wisdom —
dukkha, the origination of dukkha,
the going beyond of dukkha,
and the Noble Eightfold Path
leading to the cessation of dukkha.
This indeed is the safe refuge,
this is the highest refuge.
Having gone to this refuge,
one is liberated from all dukkha.

pali: “cattār’imāni, bhikkhave, ariya-saccāni. katamāni cattāri? dukkhaṃ ariya-saccaṃ,
en: “Bhikkhus, there are these Four Noble Truths.
What four? The noble truth of dukkha, the noble truth of the origin of dukkha, the noble truth of the cessation of dukkha, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of dukkha.
These are the Four Noble Truths.
Of these Four Noble Truths, bhikkhus,
there is a noble truth that is to be fully understood;
there is a noble truth that is to be abandoned;
there is a noble truth that is to be realized;
there is a noble truth that is to be developed.

And what, bhikkhus, is the noble truth that is to be fully understood? The noble truth of dukkha is to be fully understood; the noble truth of the origin of dukkha is to be abandoned; the noble truth of the cessation of dukkha is to be realized;
the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of dukkha is to be developed.
Therefore, bhikkhus, an exertion should be made to understand: ‘This is dukkha.’ An exertion should be made to understand: ‘This is the origin of dukkha.’
An exertion should be made to understand:
‘This is the cessation of dukkha.’
An exertion should be made to understand:
‘This is the way leading to the cessation of dukkha.’”

pali: kiñ ca, bhikkhave, jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti?
en: “Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the āsavas
is for one who knows and sees,
not for one who does not know and does not see.
For one who knows what, for one who sees what,
does the destruction of the āsavas come about?

pali: ‘ayaṃ dukkha-samudayo’ti jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkha-nirodho’ti jānato passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, ‘ayaṃ dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā’ti
en: The destruction of the āsavas comes about for one who knows and sees: ‘This is dukkha’; for one who knows and sees: ‘This is the origin of dukkha’;
for one who knows and sees: ‘This is the cessation of dukkha’; for one who knows and sees:
‘This is the way leading to the cessation of dukkha.’

pali: evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, jānato, evaṃ passato,
en: It is for one who knows thus, for one who sees thus, that the destruction of the āsavas comes about.
Therefore, bhikkhus, an exertion should be made to understand: ‘This is dukkha.’ …
An exertion should be made to understand:
‘This is the way leading to the cessation of dukkha.’”

pali: jāti’pi dukkhā, jarā’pi dukkhā, byādhi’pi dukkho,
piyehi vippayogo dukkho, yam’p’icchaṃ na labhati, tam’pi dukkhaṃ. saṃkhittena, pañc’upādāna-kkhandhā dukkhā.”
en: “Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of dukkha:
birth is dukkha, aging is dukkha, illness is dukkha,
death is dukkha; union with what is displeasing is dukkha;
separation from what is pleasing is dukkha;
not to get what one wants is dukkha;
in brief, the five clinging-aggregates are dukkha.”
One may live a hundred years
with no paññā and no samādhi.
Better it is a single day of life
for one who has paññā and meditates.
One may live a hundred years
without seeing arising and passing away.
Better it is a single day of life
for one seeing arising and passing away.
One who does not take anything as “mine”,
throughout this mind and body,
who does not sorrow over that which is not —
he is truly called a bhikkhu.
There is no fire like desire;
there is no misfortune like aversion;
there is no dukkha like the aggregates;
there is no happiness greater than peace.
Whenever one comprehends
the arising and passing away of the aggregates,
one experiences rapture and joy,
for the discerning, that [leads to] the Deathless.
“And what, bhikkhus, are the five clinging-aggregates that, in brief, are dukkha? They are:
the material form clinging-aggregate,
the vedanā clinging-aggregate, the perception
clinging-aggregate, the saṅkhāras clinging-aggregate,
and the consciousness clinging-aggregate.
These are the five clinging-aggregates that,
in brief, are dukkha.
This is called the noble truth of dukkha.”

pali: vedanā pariññeyyo dhammo; saññā pariññeyyo dhammo;
saṅkhārā pariññeyyo dhammo; viññāṇaṃ pariññeyyo dhammo; ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, pariññeyyā dhammā.”
en: “And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be fully understood? Material form, bhikkhus,
is a thing that should be fully understood;
vedanā … perception … saṅkhāras… consciousness is a thing that should be fully understood. These are called the things that should be fully understood.”

pali: ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā bārāṇasiyaṃ viharati isipatane
miga-dāye. tatra kho bhagavā pañca-vaggiye bhikkhū āmantesi: “bhikkhavo”ti.
en: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus of the group of five thus: “Bhikkhus!”—
“Venerable sir!” those bhikkhus replied.
The Blessed One said this:

pali: “rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā. rūpañ ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave,
attā abhavissa, nayidaṃ rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyya, labbhetha ca rūpe:
en: “Bhikkhus, material form is nonself.
For if, bhikkhus, form were self, this form would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible to have it of

pali: ‘evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī’ti.
en: form: ‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.’

pali: yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ anattā,
tasmā rūpaṃ ābādhāya saṃvattati, na ca labbhati rūpe:
‘evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotu, evaṃ me rūpaṃ mā ahosī’ti.
en: But because form is nonself, form leads to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of form:
‘Let my form be thus; let my form not be thus.’

pali: vedanā anattā. vedanā ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave,
attā abhavissa, nayidaṃ vedanā ābādhāya saṃvatteyya, labbhetha ca vedanāya: ‘evaṃ me vedanā hotu,
en: vedanā is nonself. For if, bhikkhus, vedanā were self, this vedanā would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible to have it of vedanā:
‘Let my vedanā be thus; let my vedanā not be thus.’

pali: yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, vedanā anattā,
tasmā vedanā ābādhāya saṃvattati, na ca labbhati vedanāya: ‘evaṃ me vedanā hotu, evaṃ me vedanā mā ahosī’ti.
en: But because vedanā is nonself, vedanā leads to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of vedanā:
‘Let my vedanā be thus; let my vedanā not be thus.’

pali: saṅkhārā ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave, attā abhavissaṃsu,
‘evaṃ me saṅkhārā hontu, evaṃ me saṅkhārā mā ahesun’ti.
yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā anattā,
‘evaṃ me saṅkhārā hontu, evaṃ me saṅkhārā mā ahesun’ti.
en: Perception is nonself …
saṅkhāras are nonself. For if, bhikkhus, saṅkhāras were self, these saṅkhāras would not lead to affliction,
and it would be possible to have it of saṅkhāras:
‘Let my saṅkhāras be thus; let my saṅkhāras not be thus.’ But because saṅkhāras are nonself,
saṅkhāras lead to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of saṅkhāras: ‘Let my saṅkhāras be thus; let my saṅkhāras not be thus.’

pali: viññāṇaṃ anattā. viññāṇañ ca h’idaṃ, bhikkhave,
attā abhavissa, nayidaṃ viññāṇaṃ ābādhāya saṃvatteyya, labbhetha ca viññāṇe:
‘evaṃ me viññāṇaṃ hotu, evaṃ me viññāṇaṃ mā ahosī’ti. yasmā ca kho, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ anattā,
‘evaṃ me viññāṇaṃ hotu, evaṃ me viññāṇaṃ mā ahosī’ti.
en: Consciousness is nonself. For if, bhikkhus, consciousness were self, this consciousness would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible to have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus;
let my consciousness not be thus.’
But because consciousness is nonself, consciousness leads to affliction, and it is not possible to have it of consciousness: ‘Let my consciousness be thus;
let my consciousness not be thus.’

pali: taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā
“yaṃ pan’āniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?
‘etaṃ mama, eso’ham asmi, eso me attā’”ti?
en: “What do you think, bhikkhus, is material form permanent or impermanent?” —
“Impermanent, venerable sir.” —
“Is what is impermanent dukkha or happiness?” —
“dukkha, venerable sir.” —
“Is what is impermanent, dukkha,
and subject to change fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” —
“No, venerable sir.”

pali: “yaṃ pan’āniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?
‘etaṃ mama, eso’ham asmi, eso me attā’”ti?
en: “Is vedanā permanent or impermanent?…
Is perception permanent or impermanent?…
Are saṅkhāras permanent or impermanent?…
Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?” — “Impermanent, venerable sir.” —
“Is what is impermanent dukkha or happiness?” —
“dukkha, venerable sir.” — “Is what is impermanent, dukkha, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” —
“No, venerable sir.”

pali: atīt’ānāgata-paccuppannaṃ, ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā, hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā,
yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ:
‘n’etaṃ mama, n’eso’ham asmi, na m’eso attā’ti
en: “Therefore, bhikkhus, any kind of material form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present,
internal or external, gross or subtle,
inferior or superior, far or near, all material form should be seen as it really is with perfect wisdom thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’

pali: yā kāci vedanā atīt’ānāgata-paccuppannā, ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, … pe … yā dūre santike vā, sabbā vedanā:
‘n’etaṃ mama, n’eso’ham asmi, na m’eso attā’ti
en: “Any kind of vedanā whatsoever …

pali: yā kāci saññā … pe … ye keci saṅkhārā
atīt’ānāgata-paccuppannā, ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā … pe … ye dūre santike vā, sabbe saṅkhārā:
‘n’etaṃ mama, n’eso’ham asmi, na m’eso attā’ti
en: Any kind of perception whatsoever …
Any kind of saṅkhāras whatsoever …

pali: ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā, oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā,
hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā, yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ: ‘n’etaṃ mama, n’eso’ham asmi, na m’eso attā’ti
en: Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external,
gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near,
all consciousness should be seen as it really is with perfect wisdom thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple experiences disenchantment towards material form,
disenchantment towards vedanā, disenchantment towards perception, disenchantment towards saṅkhāras, disenchantment towards consciousness.
Experiencing disenchantment, he becomes free from attachment. Through the fading of attachment,
he is liberated. When he is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘liberated.’
He understands: ‘Birth is finished with, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done,
there is no more for this state of being.’”

pali: idam avoca bhagavā. attamanā pañca-vaggiyā bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanduṃ.
en: That is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s statement. And while this discourse was being spoken,
the minds of the bhikkhus of the group of five were liberated from the āsavas by non-clinging.”

pali: atha kho māro pāpimā, vajirāya bhikkhuniyā
bhayaṃ, chambhitattaṃ, loma-haṃsaṃ uppādetu’kāmo, samādhimhā cāvetu’kāmo,
en: Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in the bhikkhunī Vajirā,
desiring to make her fall away from concentration, approached her and addressed her in verse:
“By whom has this being been created?
Where is the maker of the being?
Where has the being arisen?
Where does the being cease?”
“Why now do you assume ‘a being’?
Māra, have you fallen into wrong views?
This is merely a heap of saṅkhāras:
here no being is found.
Just as, with an assemblage of parts,
the word ‘chariot’ is used,
so, when the aggregates are present,
there is the convention ‘a being.’
It’s only dukkha that comes to be,
dukkha that stays and passes away.
Nothing but dukkha comes to be,
nothing but dukkha ceases.”

pali: atha kho māro pāpimā, “jānāti maṃ vajirā bhikkhunī”ti, dukkhī dummano tatthev’antaradhāyī”ti.
en: Then Māra the Evil One, realizing,
“The bhikkhunī Vajirā knows me,”
sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.”
“And how, bhikkhus, should one know, how should one see, for the immediate destruction of the āsavas to occur?

pali: idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthu-jjano, ariyānaṃ adassāvī, ariya-dhammassa akovido, ariya-dhamme avinīto, sappurisānaṃ adassāvī, sappurisa-dhammassa akovido, sappurisa-dhamme avinīto — rūpaṃ [vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ] attato samanupassati.
en: Here, bhikkhus, the uninstructed ordinary person,

who is not a seer of the noble ones and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, who is not a seer of superior persons and is unskilled and undisciplined in their Dhamma, regards material form as self.

pali: yā kho pana sā, bhikkhave, samanupassanā,
en: That regarding, bhikkhus, is a saṅkhāra. This saṅkhāra — what is its source, what is its origin,
from what is it born and produced?
When the uninstructed ordinary person experiences
what is felt, born of contact accompanied by ignorance,
craving arises: because of that, this saṅkhāra is born.

pali: evam’pi kho, bhikkhave, jānato, evaṃ passato anantarā āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.”
en: Thus, bhikkhus, that saṅkhāra is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen; that craving is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen; that vedanā is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen; that contact is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen; that ignorance is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. When one knows and sees thus, bhikkhus, the immediate destruction of the āsavas occurs.”

pali: taṃ vo pahīnaṃ, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, that which is not yours, let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha.
taṃ vo pahīnaṃ, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: And what is it, bhikkhus, that is not yours?
Material form is not yours; let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: sā vo pahīnā, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: vedanā is not yours; let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: sā vo pahīnā, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: Perception is not yours; let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: te vo pahīnā, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: saṅkhāras are not yours; let go of them.
When they have been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: taṃ vo pahīnaṃ, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: Consciousness is not yours; let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.
Suppose, bhikkhus, people were to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and foliage in this Jeta’s Grove,
or to burn them, or to do with them as they wish.
Would you think:
‘People are carrying us off, or burning us,
or doing with us as they wish’?”

pali: na hi no etaṃ, bhante, attā vā attaniyaṃ vā”ti.
en: “No, venerable sir. For what reason?
Because, venerable sir, that is neither our self
nor what belongs to our self.”
“So too, bhikkhus, material form is not yours; let go of it. When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: sā vo pahīnā, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: vedanā is not yours; let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: sā vo pahīnā, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: Perception is not yours; let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: te vo pahīnā, hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.
en: saṅkhāras are not yours; let go of them.
When they have been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.

pali: taṃ vo pahīnaṃ, hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti.
en: Consciousness is not yours; let go of it.
When it has been let go of by you,
it will be for your welfare and happiness.”
There is no fire like desire;
there is no gripping hold like hatred;
there is no snare like delusion;
there is no river like craving.
Guarding of the eye is good,
good is guarding of the ear,
guarding of the nose is good,
good is guarding of the tongue.
Guarding of the body is good,
good is guarding of speech,
guarding of the mind is good,
good is guarding everywhere.
The bhikkhu guarded everywhere
is liberated from all dukkha.

pali: taṃ ve pasahati māro, vāto rukkhaṃ’va dubbalaṃ.
en: Māra brings down one who lives contemplating attraction
in things, who is unrestrained in their senses,
not knowing moderation in food, lazy, and unenergetic —
just as wind brings down a weak tree.

pali: bhojanamhi ca mattaññuṃ, saddhaṃ āraddha-vīriyaṃ — taṃ ve na-ppasahati māro, vāto selaṃ’va pabbataṃ.
en: Māra does not bring down one who lives contemplating unattractiveness in things, who is restrained in their senses, knowing moderation in food,
full of devotion, and energetic —
just as wind does not bring down a rocky mountain.

suttas.title: indriyesu guttadvāro
suttas.en: Guarding the Doors of the Sense Faculties

pali: “kathañ ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu gutta-dvāro hoti?
idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā,
en: “And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu guard the doors of the sense faculties? Here, having seen a visual form with the eye, a bhikkhu does not grasp its marks and features.
Since, if he left the eye faculty unrestrained,
bad unwholesome states of craving and aversion
might invade him.
He practices restraint over it; he guards the eye faculty,
he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty.

pali: sotena saddaṃ sutvā… pe … ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…
jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…
en: Having heard a sound with the ear … Having smelled an odor with the nose … Having tasted a taste with the tongue … Having experienced a sensation with the body …

pali: manasā dhammaṃ viññāya, na nimitta-ggāhī hoti,
n’ānubyañjana-ggāhī; yatv’ādhikaraṇam enaṃ man’indriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ, abhijjhā-domanassā
evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu gutta-dvāro hoti.”
en: Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
a bhikkhu does not grasp its marks and features.
Since, if he left the mind faculty unrestrained,
bad unwholesome states of craving and
aversion might invade him.
He practices restraint over it; he guards the mind faculty,
he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty.
It is in this way that a bhikkhu guards the doors of the sense faculties.”

suttas.title: chappāṇakopama sutta
suttas.en: The Simile of the Six Animals

pali: “seyyathā’pi, bhikkhave, puriso aru-gatto pakka-gatto sara-vanaṃ paviseyya. tassa kusa-kaṇṭakā c’eva pāde vijjheyyuṃ, sara-pattāni ca gattāni vilekheyyuṃ. evañ hi so, bhikkhave, puriso bhiyyoso-mattāya tato-nidānaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvediyetha.
en: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man with limbs wounded and festering would enter a wood of thorny reeds, and the kusa thorns would prick his feet and the reed blades would slash his limbs. Thus that man would thereby experience even more pain and displeasure.

pali: evameva kho, bhikkhave, idh’ekacco bhikkhu gāma-gato vā arañña-gato vā labhati vattāraṃ: ‘ayañ ca so āyasmā evaṃ-kārī evaṃ-samācāro asuci-gāma-kaṇṭako’ti. taṃ ‘kaṇṭako’ti iti viditvā saṃvaro ca asaṃvaro ca veditabbo.
en: So too, bhikkhus, some bhikkhu here, gone to the village or the forest, meets someone who reproaches him thus: ‘This venerable one, acting in such a way, behaving in such a way, is a foul village thorn.’ Having understood him thus as a ‘thorn,’ one should understand restraint and non-restraint.

pali: kathañ ca, bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti? idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piya-rūpe rūpe adhimuccati, appiya-rūpe rūpe byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhita-kāya-sati ca viharati paritta-cetaso, tañ ca ceto-vimuttiṃ paññā-vimuttiṃ yathā-bhūtaṃ na-ppajānāti, yatth’assa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. sotena saddaṃ sutvā … pe … manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piya-rūpe dhamme adhimuccati, appiya-rūpe dhamme byāpajjati … pe …
en: And how, bhikkhus, is there non-restraint? Here, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is intent upon a pleasing form and repelled by a displeasing form. He dwells without having set up awareness of the body, with a limited mind, and he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, wherein those bad unwholesome states cease without remainder. Having heard a sound with the ear … Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is intent upon a pleasing mental phenomenon and repelled by a displeasing mental phenomenon …

pali: seyyathā’pi, bhikkhave, puriso cha-ppāṇake gahetvā nānā-visaye nānā-gocare daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. ahiṃ gahetvā … susumāraṃ gahetvā … pakkhiṃ gahetvā … kukkuraṃ gahetvā … siṅgālaṃ gahetvā … makkaṭaṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. daḷhāya rajjuyā bandhitvā, majjhe gaṇṭhiṃ karitvā ossajjeyya.
en: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man would catch six animals — with different domains and different feeding grounds — and tie them by a strong rope. He would catch a snake, a crocodile, a bird, a dog, a jackal, and a monkey, and tie each by a strong rope. Having done so, he would tie the ropes together with a knot in the middle and release them.

pali: atha kho te, bhikkhave, cha-ppāṇakā nānā-visayā nānā-gocarā sakaṃ sakaṃ gocara-visayaṃ āviñcheyyuṃ:
en: Then those six animals with different domains and different feeding grounds would each pull in the direction of its own feeding ground and domain.
The snake would pull one way, thinking, ‘Let me enter an anthill.’
The crocodile would pull another way, thinking, ‘Let me enter the water.’
The bird would pull another way, thinking, ‘Let me fly up into the sky.’
The dog would pull another way, thinking, ‘Let me enter a village.’
The jackal would pull another way, thinking, ‘Let me enter a charnel ground.’
The monkey would pull another way, thinking, ‘Let me enter a forest.’

pali: yadā kho te, bhikkhave, cha-ppāṇakā jhattā assu kilantā, atha kho yo nesaṃ pāṇakānaṃ balavataro assa, tassa te anuvatteyyuṃ, anuvidhāyeyyuṃ, vasaṃ gaccheyyuṃ.
en: Now when these six animals become worn out and fatigued, they would be dominated by the one among them that was strongest; they would submit to it and come under its control.

pali: evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno kāya-gatā-sati abhāvitā abahulī-katā, taṃ cakkhu āviñchati manāpiyesu rūpesu, amanāpiyā rūpā paṭikūlā honti … pe … mano āviñchati manāpiyesu dhammesu, amanāpiyā dhammā paṭikūlā honti. evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti.
en: So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has not developed and cultivated awareness directed to the body, the eye pulls in the direction of agreeable forms and disagreeable forms are repulsive … the mind pulls in the direction of agreeable mental phenomena and disagreeable mental phenomena are repulsive. It is in such a way that there is non-restraint.

pali: kathañ ca, bhikkhave, saṃvaro hoti? idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piya-rūpe rūpe n’ādhimuccati, appiya-rūpe rūpe na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhita-kāya-sati ca viharati appamāṇa-cetaso, tañ ca ceto-vimuttiṃ paññā-vimuttiṃ yathā-bhūtaṃ pajānāti, yatth’assa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti … pe … manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piya-rūpe dhamme n’ādhimuccati, appiya-rūpe dhamme na byāpajjati … pe …
en: And how, bhikkhus, is there restraint? Here, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is not intent upon a pleasing form and not repelled by a displeasing form. He dwells having set up awareness of the body, with a measureless mind, and he understands as it really is that liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, wherein those bad unwholesome states cease without remainder … Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not intent upon a pleasing mental phenomenon and not repelled by a displeasing mental phenomenon …

pali: seyyathā’pi, bhikkhave, puriso cha-ppāṇake gahetvā nānā-visaye nānā-gocare daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya … pe … daḷhāya rajjuyā bandhitvā daḷhe khīle vā thambhe vā upanibandheyya. atha kho te, bhikkhave, cha-ppāṇakā nānā-visayā nānā-gocarā sakaṃ sakaṃ gocara-visayaṃ āviñcheyyuṃ … pe …
en: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man would catch six animals — with different domains and different feeding grounds — and tie them by a strong rope … Having done so, he would bind them to a strong post or pillar. Then those six animals with different domains and different feeding grounds would each pull in the direction of its own feeding ground and domain …
